title: Allocator throttling incident synthesis and temporary playbook
content:
Summary

Short version: during a high burst evening on 2025-02-12 we observed progressive latency degradation in the dedicated GPU pools in us-west1 followed by a partial capacity blackout for low priority tenants. Root cause is allocator throttling combined with a mis-sampled scaling signal. The allocator started delaying new container assignments when internal deque metrics spiked, which amplified request queuing and caused autoscaler oscillation.

This doc captures: an incident timeline, live detection signals, a temporary playbook for oncall, quick mitigation commands, proposed permanent fixes, and follow ups owners. This is a working synthesis; please add notes under collaborators.

Context and impact

- Affected surface: Dedicated GPU pools serving hosted and dedicated customers in us-west1 region.
- User impact: p99 token latency increased from 300ms to 4.2s for several routes. Some lower tier customers saw request timeouts and automatic evictions. No customer data was leaked.
- Severity: Sev2 for dedicated customers, elevated to Sev1 internally for 90 minutes due to capacity loss.

Immediate detection and alerts that fired

- Alert SRE GPU tail latency > 1500ms across pool us-west1 for 5m (sre-alerts rule id 1302)
- Pool allocation failure rate > 2% (allocator-metrics)
- Eviction cascade warning from kube-evict monitor

High level timeline (local times PST)

- 18:01 2025-02-12: p95 and p99 start to drift up on streaming routes. First page by internal monitor.
- 18:07: Oncall sees allocation failure spikes. Slack thread started in #sre-ops.
- 18:12: Autoscaler scales down some buffer nodes based on CPU smoothing rule.
- 18:15: Allocation delays increase, queueing accumulates causing more requests to time out.
- 18:22: Evictions triggered for low priority tenants leading to tenant churn.
- 18:30: Manual intervention — increase buffer pool, pin suspected noisy tenant to quarantine pool.
- 19:05: Stabilization begins as allocation backlog cleared.
- 20:00: Post-incident triage started.

Key signals used in analysis

- allocator_dequeue_latency_seconds p95/p99 by pool
- allocator_allocation_failures_total by pool, reason label
- node_gpu_utilization_percent by node
- pod_eviction_events_total with labels tenant_id, reason
- autoscaler_scale_events with reason label and source metric

PromQL examples used during triage

- sum by(pool) (rate(allocator_allocation_failures_total[5m]))
- histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(allocator_dequeue_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool))
- max by(node) (node_gpu_utilization_percent)

Root cause hypothesis and evidence

1) Allocator backpressure trigger misfire
- Allocator uses an internal deque length as a protective backpressure signal. On 18:00 the deque metric spiked because of a transient scheduling burst from a high fanout job. The allocator entered a defensive throttling mode and started pacing assignments to worker nodes.
- Evidence: massive jump in allocator_dequeue_latency_seconds and matching increase in allocation_failures_total labeled reason=backpressure.

2) Autoscaler sampled the wrong smoothing window and interpreted short lived throughput drop as demand decrease
- The cluster autoscaler is configured to look at CPU based metrics with a 10 minute smoothing window. Because allocator pacing delayed actual container startup, the CPU signal fell and triggered a scale down before allocation backlog was cleared.
- Evidence: autoscaler_scale_events show scale down at 18:12 with reason=cpu_sustained_low while allocator_allocation_failures were increasing.

3) Eviction cascade amplified recovery time
- As evictions removed pods, remaining nodes saw redistribution and transient higher load which kept allocator deque high and prevented normal recovery until manual intervention.

Why this was different from prior incidents

- Prior incidents were noisy tenant compute hogs. This incident was primarily an internal allocator protection interaction combined with a misaligned autoscaler metric. No single tenant CPU hog was the initial trigger.

Temporary playbook for oncall (run these in order)

1) Confirm signal
- Check allocator_dequeue_latency_seconds p99 > 500ms and allocation_failures_total rising.
- Confirm p99 token latency increase on affected routes.

2) Short term containment (10-30 minutes)
- Increase dedicated buffer pool by 20-40 percent to absorb immediate influx
  - command: kubectl -n infra scale statefulset buffer-pool-us-west1 --replicas=XX  // replace XX
- If reducer tenants are known, move them to quarantine pool
  - command: airflow run infra move_tenant_to_pool --tenant=<id> --pool=quarantine-us-west1
- Disable allocator backpressure safeguard temporarily on affected allocator instances if safe
  - command: curl -X POST https://allocator-us-west1.internal/flags  -d 'disable_backpressure=true'  // internal only
  - Note: only trusted SRE and allocator team members may toggle this. Log the command in the incident channel.

3) Prevent oscillation
- Pause autoscaler driven scale down by setting scale block flag or increase smoothing window to 30m temporarily
  - command: kubectl patch configmap cluster-autoscaler-config -n kube-system --patch '{"data":{"min_smoothing_minutes":"30"}}'
- Alternatively set a temporary annotation on autoscaler: autoscaler.redwood.io/hold-scale-down=true

4) Drain and isolate suspected noisy actors
- Identify nodes with highest allocator dequeue latency and drain noncritical pods to quarantine nodes
  - command: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

5) Post mitigation validation
- Confirm allocator_dequeue_latency p99 returning to baseline and allocation_failures_total falling to near zero for 10 minute window.
- Confirm p99 token latency on user routes improved.

Quick commands and data pulls for oncall

- Get recent allocation failures: kubectl logs -l app=allocator -n infra --since=30m | grep allocation_failed | tail -100
- Query Prometheus: curl -G 'https://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(allocator_dequeue_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool))'
- Check autoscaler history: kubectl get events -n kube-system | grep cluster-autoscaler | tail -50

Post incident mitigation proposals (short, medium, long term)

Short term (1-2 weeks)
- Change autoscaler sampling to include an allocator backlog signal or extend smoothing when allocator signals are non zero. Owner: Ravi. Target: 2025-02-28.
- Add a temporary safe override flag on allocator to reduce backpressure aggressiveness when node churn is detected. Owner: Jordan. Target: 2025-02-21.

Medium term (4-8 weeks)
- Implement a composite scaling metric that accounts for allocation failures and container startup rate in addition to CPU. Owner: SRE + Platform. Target: 2025-03-28.
- Create a quarantine workflow that can be executed by oncall to quickly move tenants without full redeploy. Owner: Sofia. Target: 2025-03-10.

Long term (3 months)
- Refactor allocator to separate protective throttling from normal admission control, with graded responses and visibility. Owner: allocator team lead. Target: 2025-05-15.
- Run chaos experiments that simulate short high fanout bursts to validate autoscaler and allocator interactions. Owner: SRE QA. Target: 2025-06-01.

Observability and instrumentation changes

- Add a visible metric allocator_backpressure_mode with enum labels to show which protection mode is active.
- Emit allocator_decision_trace logs that correlate request id to allocation decisions for 5% sampling.
- Add alerting for allocation_failures_total rising while node_gpu_utilization_percent remains below 80 percent.

Ownership and follow ups (action list)

- Ravi Patel: implement autoscaler smoothing change and run config canary. Due 2025-02-28.
- Jordan Kim: add temporary allocator flag and safe toggle flow for oncall. Due 2025-02-21.
- Sofia Alvarez: build quarantine tenant runbook and simple CLI wrapper. Due 2025-03-10.
- Eliot Green: schedule chaos experiment and draft test cases. Due 2025-03-20.
- Maya Chen: prepare a short postmortem summary for weekly ops review and update this doc with any new findings. Due 2025-02-20.

Notes for retrospective meeting

- Discuss whether allocator protection should be purely reactive or predictive.
- Decide ownership model for composite scaling metric. Platform or autoscaler team.
- Evaluate whether quarantine pool should be automated or manual.

Appendix A  raw snippets observed during incident

- allocator logs sample line: allocation_failed tenant_id=tn-349 reason=backpressure deque_len=124 latency_ms=1120
- autoscaler event sample: ScaleDown: reason=cpu_sustained_low, nodes=3 -> 1 at 2025-02-12T18:12:34Z
